item.title: Real-world use of digital therapeutics for substance use disorders in primary care: Observational study of the engagement cascade by substance type
item.description:
Background: Patient engagement with digital therapeutics for substance use disorder (SUD) in primary care remains poorly understood. We analyzed engagement in routine care and whether specific types of substance use are associated with greater engagement.

Methods: This real-world observational study analyzed 83 primary care patients prescribed reSET® or reSET-O®, US Food and Drug Administration-authorized digital therapeutics for SUD. Substance types (unhealthy alcohol, cannabis, and other drug use) were identified from routine health screens and clinical diagnoses. The primary outcome was progression through four engagement cascade milestones: app activation, user guide completion, completion of ≥ one module, and treatment completion. Vendor logfiles provided weekly module counts. Logistic regression evaluated associations between substance use and engagement, adjusting for age and sex.

Results: Overall, 50.6% of patients activated the app, 45.8% completed the guide, 38.6% completed ≥ one module, and 13.3% met the vendor-defined treatment completion criterion. Among those who activated it, the median number of modules completed was 4 (interquartile range 1-32); half of module users stopped by week 4. Unhealthy alcohol use was associated with higher odds of app activation, user guide completion, and completion of ≥ one module (adjusted odds ratios [95% confidence intervals] = 2.84 [1.10-7.66], 3.48 [1.32-9.82], and 3.67 [1.32-11.26], respectively). Cannabis and other drug use were not associated with engagement milestones.

Conclusions: Engagement with prescription-based digital therapeutics in primary care varies by substance type and is concentrated in the first month of use. Overall, engagement remains limited. Future research should validate these findings and refine engagement strategies.

Idrisov B, Idu A, Key D, Bobb JF, Glass JE

item.title: Medication for opioid use disorder following urine drug testing: An observational cohort study of linked national laboratory and medical and pharmacy claims data
item.description:
Background and aims: Urine drug testing (UDT) is commonly used in opioid use disorder (OUD) care to assess substance use and inform clinical decision-making, yet little is known about how opioid UDT results are associated with subsequent medication for opioid (MOUD) use and adherence. This study examines the association between opioid UDT, post-UDT MOUD use, and treatment adherence using linked national laboratory and medical and pharmacy claims data.

Design: Retrospective quantitative observational cohort study.

Setting: United States, using linked national laboratory and adjudicated medical and pharmacy claims data covering all 50 states and Washington DC.

Participants: Adults aged 18-64 years with at least one opioid UDT between June 2017 and May 2025 and continuous medical and pharmacy enrollment for 180 days prior and 365 days following the initial test (N = 759,153).

Measurement: Primary outcomes were post-UDT MOUD use within 365 days after opioid UDT and MOUD adherence. Treatment adherence was defined using claims-based gaps consistent with prior literature. Multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for demographics, insurance type, comorbid mental and physical health conditions, prior MOUD use, and state-level fixed effects.

Findings: Overall, 32.1% of patients tested positive for opioid use. Post-UDT MOUD use was low (5.3% overall; 9.4% among those with positive opioid UDT). Multivariable logistic regression modeling showed that a positive opioid UDT was associated with more than twice the odds of post-UDT MOUD use (OR = 2.15; 95% CI = 2.10-2.20). However, among patients with post-UDT MOUD, positive opioid UDT was associated with lower odds of MOUD adherence (OR = 0.51; 95% CI = 0.49-0.54). Results were consistent for patients with diagnosed OUD.

Conclusions: Positive opioid UDT was associated with increased likelihood of post-UDT MOUD use but low MOUD treatment adherence. These findings highlight opportunities to strengthen sustained engagement with evidence-based treatment and underscore the need for care models that better support patients following opioid UDT, including timely MOUD use and adherence support.

White B, Skinner J, Hammonds T, Bhattacharyya P, Ali MM

item.title: Sociodemographic and intersecting sociodemographic subgroups in relation to US adult tobacco use trajectories over a 10-year period: Analysis of Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) data
item.description:
Introduction: Limited research has assessed tobacco use trajectories among subpopulations, particularly those representing intersecting minority identities, across adulthood. This study assessed tobacco use trajectories over 10 years among sociodemographic subgroups of US adults.

Methods: We analyzed 7 waves of data (2013-2022) from the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH). General growth mixture modeling assessed trajectories of any past-month use of cigarettes, e-cigarettes, cigars, hookah, and smokeless tobacco. Multivariable multinomial logistic regression assessed sociodemographics and sociodemographic interactions in relation to trajectory.

Results: Four trajectories were identified: "consistently low" (68.0% of participants) with low prevalence over time (0.7%-2.7 "consistently high" (21.6%) with 95-99% using at each wave; "medium increasing" (4.5%) which increased from 23% using at W1-60% at W7; and "steep decreasing" (5.9%) which decreased from 88% using at W1-6% at W7. Factors associated with being in the latter 3 trajectories vs. "consistently low" included being younger, male, sexual minority (SM), Black, and less educated. Factors associated with "steep decreasing" or "consistently high" vs. "medium increasing" included being older and White vs. Black; being male, non-Hispanic, and less educated was also associated with "consistently high". Factors associated with "consistently high" vs. "steep decreasing" included being older, non-Hispanic, and less educated. Significant interactions indicated certain intersecting identities (e.g., female and SM, SM and Black, Black/another race and Hispanic) more likely showed the latter 3 trajectories.

Conclusion: Tobacco prevention and intervention efforts must attend to sociodemographic profiles of adults at greatest risk for persistent or escalating tobacco use.

Wang Y, Thakkar S, Romm KF, Yang YT, Berg CJ

item.title: Nationwide trends of six medications for alcohol use disorder prescriptions post-discharge in patients hospitalized with alcohol-associated liver disease between 2015 and 2024
item.description:
Introduction: Alcohol associated liver disease (ALD) carries a high risk of hospitalization and recidivism, yet post-discharge medications for alcohol use disorder (MAUD) are not universally prescribed. MAUD prescriptions have been associated with reduced recidivism and hepatic decompensation. However, national data on prescribing patterns is limited. We examined ten-year trends in six MAUD prescriptions after hospitalization for ALD.

Methods: We identified 150,241 US adults hospitalized with ALD between 2015 and 2024 using electronic health records from TriNetX. Outcomes included annual prevalence, incidence rate, and incidence proportion of post-discharge MAUD prescriptions. FDA-approved agents included disulfiram, acamprosate, and naltrexone; off-label agents included topiramate, baclofen, and gabapentin. Trends were assessed using Joinpoint regression with annual percentage change (APC) and average annual percentage change (AAPC). Subgroup analyses were stratified by cirrhosis status and sex.

Results: FDA-approved MAUD had consistently lower prescription rates than off-label agents over the past decade. From 2015-2024, disulfiram was the only FDA-approved agent with a declining trend, while acamprosate (AAPC 20.35%) and naltrexone (AAPC 17.83%) demonstrated significant increases for new prescriptions. By 2024, the prevalence of FDA-approved and off-label MAUD prescriptions were 17.98% and 41.96%, respectively. Patients with cirrhosis had lower prescribing rates but exhibited greater relative increases in FDA-approved MAUD prescriptions. Women were more likely to receive off-label prescriptions, though both sexes showed similar upward trends.

Conclusion: Post-discharge MAUD prescribing for ALD has risen significantly, but less than 20% of patients receive FDA-approved MAUD. Expanding access to evidence-based medications is critical to improve outcomes in this high-risk population.

Chan SY, Yeo YH, Yang HY, Zhang W, Ting PS

item.title: Incidence of opioid use disorder among patients prescribed long-term opioid therapy: An observational study
item.description:
Background: There are no estimates of incident opioid use disorder (OUD), using current diagnostic criteria, among patients prescribed long-term opioid therapy (LtOT). The U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a postmarketing requirement to estimate the 12-month incidence of OUD among patients receiving LtOT.

Methods: Study 3033-1 was a prospective, observational cohort study conducted in 10 health systems with one year of follow up. Data were collected August 2017 to October 2021, analyses were completed December 2025. The primary outcome was pain-adjusted, moderate to severe DSM-5 OUD involving prescription opioids measured using the Psychiatric Research Interview for Substance and Mental Disorders, adapted for assessing OUD among patients treated with opioids (PRISM-5-OP). Secondary outcomes included moderate to severe DSM-5 OUD without pain adjustment and any OUD involving prescription opioids with and without pain adjustment. Overall and stratified incidence were calculated.

Results: 1952 participants were included; 76% were aged 50 + ; 58% were female, 80% were White. The 12-month incidence of the primary outcome was 1.54%, the outcome without pain adjustment resulted in an incidence of 4.46%. Incidence of any DSM-5 OUD involving prescription opioids was 6.92% with pain adjustment and 18.14% without pain adjustment. Incidence estimates were similar across age, sex, and Medicaid status. Some estimates were higher among those with past-year or prior to past-year substance use or major depressive disorders.

Conclusions: At one year, the incidence of at least moderate OUD ranged from 1.54% to 4.46%. These findings can inform clinician and patient shared decision-making and evaluations of OUD prevention efforts.

Trial registration: NCT02751762.

Yarborough BJH, Smith N, Stumbo SP, Janoff S, Keast E, Wartko PD

item.title: County-level context and differential policy impacts on buprenorphine use among medicaid enrollees with opioid use disorder in Kentucky, 2018-2025
item.description:
Purpose: To estimate changes in buprenorphine use among Kentucky Medicaid enrollees with opioid use disorder (OUD) after policy changes and pandemic disruptions, and whether impacts differed by county-level context, primarily rurality and, secondarily, opioid treatment program (OTP) availability.

Methods: We analyzed Kentucky Medicaid claims from January 2018 through June 2025, identifying enrollees with diagnosed OUD to construct 10,800 county-month observations. Logistic regression fitted with weighted generalized estimating equations was used for statistical modeling of an interrupted time series (ITS) design to assess changes in the monthly proportion of enrollees with OUD receiving buprenorphine. Interruptions included removal of prior authorization (PA) requirements for transmucosal buprenorphine, methadone coverage initiation, COVID-19-related policy changes, and federal X-waiver elimination. Rurality and OTP availability were evaluated as effect modifiers.

Results: The proportion of enrollees with OUD receiving buprenorphine increased from 0.29 to 0.45 across the study period. PA removal was associated with an immediate increase in the odds of buprenorphine use (odds ratio [OR]=1.043; 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.025, 1.061), corresponding to a 1.4-percentage-point increase. X-waiver elimination was associated with a sustained increase in trend (OR 1.007; 95% CI 1.004-1.010). Differential effects by rurality were limited to the COVID-19 period. Counties without an OTP responded more strongly to PA removal than counties with an OTP (P = 0.037).

Conclusions: Removal of administrative and regulatory barriers was associated with increased buprenorphine use among Kentucky Medicaid enrollees with OUD, with effects varying by county-level context, particularly OTP availability.

Miracle DK, Slavova S, Freeman PR, Tarima S

item.title: Associations between kratom (Mitragyna Speciosa) use and real-time anxiety and sadness: A 15-day ecological momentary assessment study
item.description:
Background: Kratom (Mitragyna Speciosa) is increasingly used in the U.S. for self-management of pain and mental health symptoms, yet its real-time effects on emotional distress remain poorly understood. We used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to examine momentary associations of kratom use with anxiety and sadness.

Methods: A secondary analysis was conducted among 357 adult kratom consumers who adults who consume kratom completed a 15-day EMA protocol. Multilevel models assessed whether kratom use events occurring within the prior 180min were associated with momentary anxiety and sadness, and whether these associations were moderated by past 30-day use of prescribed anxiolytic or antidepressant medications.

Results: After adjusting for covariates, both single and multiple kratom use events in the previous 180min were associated with lower momentary anxiety compared to no use. For sadness, only single use events were significantly associated with lower scores. Past 30-day prescribed anxiolytic and antidepressant use did not significantly moderate these associations. Higher baseline anxiety and depressive symptoms were associated with greater momentary anxiety and sadness across the 15-day study period.

Conclusions: Kratom use was associated with small reductions in anxiety and, to a lesser extent, sadness in naturalistic settings. These associations were not influenced by past 30-day history of anxiolytic and antidepressant use. These results highlight kratom's potential role in real-time self-management of emotional distress while underscoring the need for randomized controlled trials and longitudinal studies to determine its clinical significance and long-term impact on mental health.

Timmons P, Daniulaityte R, Panlilio LV, Smith KE, Epstein DH, Mun CJ
